paras: The attempted lynching of Jesus Leon was an effort in June 1881 at San Juan Capistrano, California, to lynch Leon, a man described as "a Mexican" who was accused of stabbing Enlogio Alvarez to death. Officers prevented the attempt and took Leon to jail in Los Angeles, where he was charged with murder the following month.

According to a telegraphic report, Leon was accused of murdering Enlogio Alvarez at San Juan Capistrano by stabbing him with a knife. The report gives no date for the stabbing, and Alvarez's race is not stated.

While Leon was a prisoner at Capistrano, "a desperate attempt to lynch the prisoner was made," but it "was prevented by the officers." The report does not identify the would-be lynchers, their number, the site, or the time of day. Leon was then brought to Los Angeles and lodged in jail.

On July 11, 1881, an information charging Jesus Leon with murder was filed in the Los Angeles Superior Court before Judge Sepulveda, with no bail allowed. Arraignment of all prisoners in custody was set for the following Monday. No report of arrests of the would-be lynchers, of an inquest into Alvarez's death, or of the outcome of Leon's trial was found in the coverage.

The attempt is known from a single sentence in a column of "Telegraphic Items" printed by The Silver State of Unionville, Nevada, on June 18, 1881, between news of Irish agitation and Virginia politics. The item identified Leon only as "a Mexican" and offered no comment on the mob or the officers. The Los Angeles Herald's court column of July 12 recorded the case only as "People vs. Jesus Leon—Murder," without mention of the lynching attempt.
